فَأَمَرَهُمُ النَّبِيُّ صلى الله عليه وسلم بِلِقَاحٍ وَأَنْ يَشْرَبُوا مِنْ أَبْوَالِهَا وَأَلْبَانِهَا
The Prophet prescribes camel urine and milk as medicine
النبي يصف أبوال الإبل وألبانها دواءً
صحيح البخاري ٢٣٣ · صحيح مسلم ١٦٧١ · سنن النسائي ٤٠٣١
Bukhari 233البخاري ٢٣٣ Muslim 1671aمسلم ١٦٧١أ Nasa'i 4031النسائي ٤٠٣١ WHO advice on MERSنصيحة منظمة الصحة العالمية

In Bukhari 233 (Anas) some people of the 'Ukl or 'Uraynah tribe came to Medina and "its climate did not suit them." The Prophet ordered them to go to a herd of milch camels and drink their milk and urine as a remedy, and they recovered (the same report is in Muslim 1671 and Nasa'i 4031). Camel urine has no demonstrated curative effect, and drinking it carries risk: in its MERS-CoV guidance the WHO advises "people should avoid drinking raw camel milk, camel urine or eating meat that has not been thoroughly cooked." Classical scholars were divided. Malik and Ahmad held that the urine of edible animals is pure, while Abu Hanifa, Shafi'i and the majority held all urine impure and permitted this treatment only as a necessity or a special case. Al-Ayni argued the Prophet was acting on revelation about these men's cure, so the ruling may not extend to ordinary cases. The objection is that the oldest and most reliable hadith collections present urine as a prescribed medicine for sickness, and a Muslim who follows the example literally is exposed to disease.

في البخاري ٢٣٣ عن أنس أن ناساً من عُكل أو عُرينة قدموا المدينة فاجتووها (لم يوافقهم مناخها)، فأمرهم النبي بلقاح (إبل حلوب) وأن يشربوا من أبوالها وألبانها دواءً فبرؤوا (والخبر نفسه في مسلم ١٦٧١ والنسائي ٤٠٣١). ولم يثبت لبول الإبل أثر شافٍ، وفي شربه خطر: فمنظمة الصحة العالمية في إرشادها بشأن متلازمة الشرق الأوسط التنفسية (ميرس) تنصح بأن «يتجنب الناس شرب حليب الإبل النيء أو بولها أو أكل اللحم غير المطبوخ جيداً». وقد اختلف العلماء القدماء: فعند مالك وأحمد بول مأكول اللحم طاهر، وعند أبي حنيفة والشافعي والجمهور البول كله نجس وأجازوا هذا العلاج للضرورة أو حالة خاصة. وقال العيني إن النبي كان يعمل بوحي في شفاء هؤلاء الرجال فلا يتعدى الحكم إلى الحالات العادية. والاعتراض أن أقدم كتب الحديث وأوثقها تعرض البول دواءً موصوفاً للمرض، وأن من اقتدى حرفياً يعرّض نفسه للمرض.

Direct quoteScience

Internal Contradictionsالتناقضات الداخلية

🔄 Internal Contradiction

A perfect, uncreated text cannot contain factual, mathematical, and historical paradoxes. Scholars rely heavily on "abrogation" (Naskh) to excuse Allah constantly changing his mind, but factual errors cannot be abrogated.

النص الكامل والمثالي لا يمكن أن يحتوي على تناقضات رياضية أو تاريخية. يعتمد رجال الدين على قاعدة "النسخ" لتبرير التناقضات، لكن الحقائق والتسلسل الزمني والأحداث التاريخية لا يمكن "نسخها".

🎭
قُلْ كُلٌّ مِّنْ عِندِ اللَّهِ
Is Evil from God or from Man?
هل الشر من الله أم من الإنسان؟
٤:٧٨ ضد ٤:٧٩
Quran 4:78القرآن ٤:٧٨ Quran 4:79القرآن ٤:٧٩

4:78 explicitly says "All things [good and evil] are from Allah." The VERY NEXT verse, 4:79, contradicts this completely, stating "Whatever comes to you of good is from Allah, but whatever comes to you of evil is from yourself." A literal back-to-back theological paradox.

الآية ٤:٧٨ تقول بوضوح "قُلْ كُلٌّ مِّنْ عِندِ اللَّهِ" (الحسنة والسيئة). وفي الآية التي تليها مباشرة ٤:٧٩ تقول "وَمَا أَصَابَكَ مِن سَيِّئَةٍ فَمِن نَّفْسِكَ". تناقض حرفي متتالي في تحديد المصدر الفعلي للشر.

Direct quoteContradict
👹
إِلَّا إِبْلِيسَ كَانَ مِنَ الْجِنِّ
Iblis: Angel or Jinn?
طبيعة إبليس: مَلَك أم جني؟
٢:٣٤ ضد ١٨:٥٠
Quran 2:34القرآن ٢:٣٤ Quran 18:50القرآن ١٨:٥٠

2:34 states God commanded the *angels* to prostrate, and they all did "except Iblis," grammatically categorizing him as a rebellious angel. However, 18:50 explicitly states "he was of the *jinn*." The standard reply is that Iblis was a jinn who was in the angels' company and was therefore addressed by the command, making "except Iblis" a disconnected exception (a reading attributed to Hasan al-Basri, who said Iblis was never an angel). It is needed because 66:6 says angels "do not disobey Allah in what He commands them." Other commentators took Iblis as an angel of a jinn tribe. The objection is that 2:34 reads most naturally as an exception from the angels.

الآية ٢:٣٤ تقول "وَإِذْ قُلْنَا لِلْمَلَائِكَةِ اسْجُدُوا لِآدَمَ فَسَجَدُوا إِلَّا إِبْلِيسَ"، وهو استثناء يصنفه لغوياً كأحد الملائكة. لكن الآية ١٨:٥٠ تصرح بوضوح "كَانَ مِنَ الْجِنِّ". تضارب جلي في أصل المخلوق. والرد المعتاد أن إبليس جني كان في صحبة الملائكة فشمله الأمر، فيكون «إِلَّا إِبْلِيسَ» استثناءً منقطعاً (وهو قول منسوب إلى الحسن البصري الذي قال إن إبليس لم يكن ملكاً قط). وهذا ضروري لأن ٦٦:٦ تقول إن الملائكة «لَّا يَعْصُونَ اللَّهَ مَا أَمَرَهُمْ». وعدّه آخرون ملكاً من قبيلة من الجن. والاعتراض أن ٢:٣٤ تُقرأ بأبسط معانيها استثناءً من الملائكة.

✝️
إِنِّي مُتَوَفِّيكَ وَرَافِعُكَ إِلَيَّ
Did Jesus actually die?
هل مات المسيح حقاً؟
١٩:٣٣، ٣:٥٥ ضد ٤:١٥٧
Quran 19:33القرآن ١٩:٣٣ Quran 3:55القرآن ٣:٥٥ Quran 4:157القرآن ٤:١٥٧

19:33 and 3:55 explicitly quote Jesus speaking of the day he "dies" and Allah promising to cause his physical death (mutawaffeeka). Yet 4:157 strictly denies he ever died or was killed, claiming it was only "made to appear so" (shubbiha lahum).

الآيات ١٩:٣٣ و ٣:٥٥ تتحدث بوضوح عن "موت" و"وفاة" عيسى الحقيقية (إني متوفيك). في حين تنفي الآية ٤:١٥٧ موته أو صلبه قطعياً وتقول "شُبِّهَ لَهُمْ".

Bukhari 5707 (Abu Hurayra) joins two statements in one narration: there is no 'adwa (contagion), no bad omen from birds, no hamah and no bad omen in the month of Safar, and "one should run away from the leper as one runs away from a lion." The first line denies that disease spreads, and the second treats leprosy as something to flee. The traditional reconciliation is that the first line denies that sickness spreads by itself without Allah's will, as the pagan Arabs believed, while the second is a precaution, since Allah makes the spread happen. Critics reply that the hadith gives no hint of this distinction, and that infectious disease does spread from person to person by known microbes.

Ibn Mas'ud was one of the Prophet's closest companions and a leading Quran teacher. Other reports (Ahmad, Ibn Hibban) say he did not write them in his copy. Ibn Hazm called the reports fabricated and Nawawi called them false, but Ibn Hajar said the report of scraping them out is explicit and authentic, and Ibn Kathir and Suyuti accepted it. Defenders say Ibn Mas'ud thought them protective prayers, or that nothing should be written in the mushaf without the Prophet's permission, and that the community's later agreement settles the question. The objection is that the text claims to be preserved (15:9), and the early companion with the best claim to know it is reported to have rejected two of its surahs.

Bukhari 1145 (Abu Hurayra; Sahih): "Our Lord, the Blessed, the Superior, comes down every night to the nearest heaven when the last third of the night remains," and says: "Is there anyone to invoke Me, so that I may respond? Is there anyone to ask Me, so that I may grant him his request? Is there anyone seeking My forgiveness, so that I may forgive him?" Because the Earth is a rotating sphere, the last third of the night is always occurring somewhere, so the descent would never stop and Allah would be permanently at the lowest heaven, which sits uneasily with the Quran's picture of Him settled on the Throne (20:5). Mainstream scholars answer that Allah descends in a way that befits Him and that we do not ask how, and some modern readers treat the language as figurative. The objection is that a literal act of motion in time sits badly with a being outside time, and with "there is nothing like Him" (42:11).

Mary (Jesus' mother, 1st century) is explicitly called "Sister of Aaron" (Moses' brother, 1400 BCE). The author confused them because both are named Maryam/Miriam. Apologists claim "sister" means descendant, but Mary was of the Tribe of Judah, not Levi (Aaron's tribe). The standard Muslim reply comes from a hadith (Muslim 2135): the Christians of Najran challenged Mughira ibn Shu'ba on this verse, and the Prophet told him that people used to name their children after earlier prophets and righteous people, so this "Aaron" would be another man of that name. The objection is that the verse addresses Mary as sister of Aaron and in the same sentence says "your father was not a man of evil" (19:28), and neither it nor the hadith identifies any such man. Some apologists add that Luke 1:5 and 1:36 link Mary's relative Elizabeth to the daughters of Aaron.

The author presents the "Seven Sleepers of Ephesus" (a widely circulated Christian fairy-tale about youths magically sleeping in a cave for 309 years to escape persecution) as literal, divine historical fact. The same legend circulated in Syriac Christianity: the bishop Jacob of Serugh (died 521 CE) wrote a homily on the sleepers of Ephesus, about a century before the Quran. 18:22 itself lists differing counts ("three, the fourth their dog", "five", "seven and the eighth their dog") and says Allah knows best. A parallel appears in the Jewish midrash Pirke de-Rabbi Eliezer (chapter 21, Friedlander's 1916 translation, p. 156): a raven buries its dead companion, and Adam, who did not know how to bury Abel, copies it. The two versions differ on who is taught (Adam in the midrash, Cain in the Quran). The direction of influence is disputed. Pirke de-Rabbi Eliezer is generally dated to the 8th or 9th century, after the Quran, and Muslim writers argue the borrowing could have run the other way. Critics respond that the midrash probably preserves older traditions, and that the raven story fits the pattern of other biblical-story parallels in the Quran. The story is never told in full in the Quran. Classical Muslim commentators filled in the story with details that Ibn Kathir regarded as largely fabricated and traced to Ka'b al-Ahbar. Apologists say the verse describes real angels in a test, not a borrowing. The objection is that an angelic school of sorcery in Babylon is a late-antique Near Eastern motif whose full form appears in non-Islamic traditions, and that Muslim tradition itself could not agree on what the verse means.

زواج عائشة بنت تسع سنوات — القرآن يُنظِّمه
٦٥:٤ (الطلاق) · البخاري ٣٨٩٤ / مسلم ١٤٢٢
Quran 65:4القرآن ٦٥:٤ Bukhari 3894البخاري ٣٨٩٤ Muslim 1422مسلم ١٤٢٢

Quran 65:4 sets waiting-period (iddah) rules for wives "who have not yet menstruated" — explicitly legislating divorce procedures for pre-pubescent child wives. Bukhari 3894 and Muslim 1422 confirm Muhammad consummated his marriage to Aisha when she was 9 years old. The Quran does not prohibit child marriage; it actively regulates its dissolution. This is the "perfect, eternal moral law."

تُحدد الآية (٦٥:٤) عدة الطلاق للزوجات «اللائي لم يحضن» — أي القاصرات قبل البلوغ — مما يُشرّع صريحاً زواج الأطفال ويُنظّم طلاقهن. ويؤكد البخاري (٣٨٩٤) ومسلم (١٤٢٢) أن النبي دخل بعائشة وهي ابنة تسع سنوات. القرآن لا يحظر زواج الأطفال، بل يُنظّم إجراءاته التشريعية.

The Quran condemns same-sex relations through the story of Lot, calling it the vilest act of any "people in the world." The Prophet commanded: "Kill the one who does it, and the one to whom it is done" (Abu Dawud 4462, Tirmidhi 1456). All four Sunni schools mandate capital punishment. This makes state execution of gay people a direct, un-abrogated divine mandate — not a medieval aberration.

يُدين القرآن العلاقات المثلية عبر قصة لوط، واصفاً إياها بأنها أبشع فاحشة في «العالمين». وأمر النبي صراحةً: «من وجدتموه يعمل عمل قوم لوط فاقتلوا الفاعل والمفعول به» (أبو داود ٤٤٦٢). المذاهب الأربعة تُوجب الإعدام. إعدام المثليين إذن فريضة دينية أبدية غير منسوخة.

When asked about the fate of children of polytheists, Muhammad replied: "Allah knows best what they would have done" (Bukhari 1384), implying God foreknows their damnation and creates them destined for Hell regardless. The "Most Merciful" predestines infants to eternal fire based on the religion of their parents.

يُقرر القرآن (٩٨:٦) أن جميع الكافرين من أهل الكتاب والمشركين في نار جهنم خالدين فيها. وحين سُئل النبي عن أطفال المشركين، أجاب: «الله أعلم بما كانوا عاملين» (البخاري ١٣٨٤)، مما يعني أن الله يعلم مسبقاً مصيرهم في الجحيم ويخلقهم مقدّرين له. «أرحم الراحمين» يقدّر الأطفال للنار الأبدية بسبب دين آبائهم.

Eyes branded, limbs cut off, water denied until death
قطع الأطراف وسمل الأعين ومنع الماء حتى الموت
صحيح البخاري ٢٣٣ / ٦٨٠٢ · صحيح مسلم ١٦٧١ · سنن النسائي ٤٠٣١ / ٤٠٣٤ · سنن ابن ماجه ٢٥٧٨ · سنن أبي داود ٤٣٦٤
Bukhari 233البخاري ٢٣٣ Bukhari 6802البخاري ٦٨٠٢ Muslim 1671aمسلم ١٦٧١ Nasa'i 4031النسائي ٤٠٣١ Nasa'i 4034النسائي ٤٠٣٤ Ibn Majah 2578ابن ماجه ٢٥٧٨ Abu Dawud 4364أبو داود ٤٣٦٤

Men of 'Ukl / 'Uraynah fell ill in Medina and Muhammad told them to drink the urine and milk of the zakat camels as medicine. After they recovered they killed the shepherd and drove off the camels. Anas reports the punishment: "He had their hands and feet cut off, their eyes gouged out (or branded with heated nails), and left them in Al-Harrah. They asked for water and were not given any" (Bukhari 233, 6802; Muslim 1671; Nasa'i 4031; Abu Dawud 4364). Ibn Majah 2578 and Nasa'i 4034 add that they were seen biting the ground from thirst until they died. Their crime was murder and robbery (hirabah), for which Quran 5:33 prescribes execution, crucifixion or amputation, but the method here was deliberate torture: blinding, mutilation, wounds left uncauterised, and refusal of water to the dying. The same hadith also records the prophetic prescription of camel urine as medicine. Some jurists argue the blinding was retaliation for what they did to the shepherd, and others that it was later abrogated, but the narrations themselves are in the major collections.

قدم رهط من عُكل أو عُرينة المدينة فاستوخموها، فأمرهم النبي بشرب أبوال إبل الصدقة وألبانها دواءً. فلما صحّوا قتلوا الراعي واستاقوا الإبل. يروي أنس العقوبة: «فقطع أيديهم وأرجلهم وسمل أعينهم (أو كحلها بمسامير محماة)، وألقوا في الحرة، يستسقون فلا يُسقون» (البخاري ٢٣٣، ٦٨٠٢، مسلم ١٦٧١، النسائي ٤٠٣١، أبو داود ٤٣٦٤). وفي ابن ماجه ٢٥٧٨ والنسائي ٤٠٣٤ أنهم كانوا يعضون الأرض بأفواههم من العطش حتى ماتوا. جريمتهم القتل والسطو (الحرابة)، وعقوبتها في الآية ٥:٣٣ القتل أو الصلب أو القطع، لكن الأسلوب كان تعذيباً متعمداً: سمل الأعين وبتر الأطراف وترك الجروح دون كي ومنع الماء عن المحتضرين. ويفيد الحديث نفسه بوصف أبوال الإبل دواءً. ويرى بعض الفقهاء أن السمل كان قصاصاً بما فعلوه بالراعي، ويرى آخرون أنه نُسخ، لكن الروايات نفسها في كتب الحديث الكبرى.

"They are from them": women and children in night raids
نساؤهم وأطفالهم في الغارات الليلية: «هم منهم»
صحيح مسلم ١٧٤٥
Muslim 1745aمسلم ١٧٤٥ Muslim 1745bمسلم ١٧٤٥ب Muslim 1745cمسلم ١٧٤٥ج

Al-Sa'b ibn Jaththama reports that Muhammad was asked about the women and children of the polytheists who are struck in night raids, and he said: "They are from them" (Muslim 1745a, 1745b). Another route has "They are from their fathers" (Muslim 1745c). Muslim titles the chapter "Permissibility of killing women and children in night raids, so long as it is not done deliberately", and other hadiths forbid targeting women and children directly. The result is a rule that treats civilian deaths in a raid on sleeping villagers as collateral rather than a crime: the children share the legal status of their fathers. Apologists say the saying only means they take the same ruling while the raid is happening, and that other narrations forbid killing them on purpose.

روى الصعب بن جثامة أن النبي سُئل عن أهل الدار من المشركين يُبيَّتون فيصاب من نسائهم وذراريهم، فقال: «هم منهم» (مسلم ١٧٤٥أ، ١٧٤٥ب). وفي رواية أخرى: «هم من آبائهم» (مسلم ١٧٤٥ج). وبوّب مسلم الباب: «جواز قتل النساء والصبيان في البيات من غير تعمد»، وتنهى أحاديث أخرى عن قصدهم. فالنتيجة قاعدة تعامل موت المدنيين في غارة على نيام آمنين كأثر جانبي لا جريمة، إذ يأخذ الأطفال حكم آبائهم. ويقول المدافعون إن المعنى أنهم في الحكم سواء أثناء الغارة، وإن روايات أخرى تحرم قتلهم عمداً.

Pregnant woman stoned after weaning her baby
رجم الغامدية بعد فطام رضيعها
صحيح مسلم ١٦٩٥ · سنن أبي داود ٤٤٤٢
Muslim 1695aمسلم ١٦٩٥أ Muslim 1695bمسلم ١٦٩٥ب Abu Dawud 4442أبو داود ٤٤٤٢

A woman of the Ghamid tribe came to Muhammad and confessed to adultery; he sent her away. She returned, pregnant, and said "Perhaps you want to send me away as you sent away Ma'iz" (Muslim 1695). He ordered her to leave until she gave birth, then to return after she had weaned the infant. She came back with the child holding a piece of bread, the child was handed to a Muslim, and "she was put in a ditch up to her chest and he commanded the people and they stoned her" (Muslim 1695b; Abu Dawud 4442). Muhammad prayed over her and said her repentance would be accepted even from a tax collector. The details matter: no witnesses, no accuser, a voluntary confession she repeated, and still the penalty was death by stoning of a mother. A Sahih-graded precedent for execution by stoning of a mother, after which her child was raised by another family.

جاءت امرأة من غامد إلى النبي واعترفت بالزنا فردّها. ثم عادت حاملاً وقالت: «لعلك أن تردني كما رددت ماعز بن مالك» (مسلم ١٦٩٥). فأمرها بالذهاب حتى تلد، ثم بإرضاعه حتى تفطمه. فجاءت بالصبي في يده كسرة خبز، فدُفع الصبي إلى رجل من المسلمين، «وحُفر لها إلى صدرها وأمر الناس فرجموها» (مسلم ١٦٩٥ب، أبو داود ٤٤٤٢). وصلى عليها النبي وقال إنها تابت توبة لو تابها صاحب مكس لغُفر له. والتفاصيل مهمة: لا شهود ولا مشتكٍ، اعتراف طوعي كررته، ومع ذلك كانت العقوبة رجم أم حتى الموت. سابقة صحيحة الإسناد لتنفيذ الرجم بأم، ثم نشأ ولدها في أسرة أخرى.

Man stabs his slave-mother for insulting Muhammad; her blood is wasted
قتل أم الولد لسبّ النبي ودمها هدر
سنن أبي داود ٤٣٦١ · سنن النسائي ٤٠٧٥
Abu Dawud 4361أبو داود ٤٣٦١ Nasa'i 4075النسائي ٤٠٧٥

Ibn Abbas reports that a blind man had a slave-mother (umm walad) who used to insult the Prophet. He forbade her and rebuked her but she would not stop. One night, he said: "I took a dagger, put it on her belly and pressed it till I killed her." A child who had come between her legs was smeared with her blood. In the morning the man confessed to the Prophet, who said: "Bear witness: no retaliation is payable for her blood" (Sunan Abi Dawud 4361, graded Sahih by Al-Albani; parallel in Nasa'i 4075). A man killed the mother of his own children, a slave woman he owned, for speech, and Muhammad cancelled even the blood-money. Classical jurists cite this report as a key proof-text for killing blasphemers. Other versions of the story (Abu Dawud 4362, graded weak in chain) describe a Jewish woman who was strangled, which scholars discuss as either the same story or a different one.

روى ابن عباس أن أعمى كانت له أم ولد تشتم النبي وتقع فيه، فينهاها فلا تنتهي ويزجرها فلا تنزجر. فلما كانت ذات ليلة قال: «فأخذت المِغْوَل فوضعته في بطنها واتكأت عليها حتى قتلتها». وتلطخ بدمها طفل كان بين رجليها. فلما أصبح أخبر النبي، فقال: «ألا اشهدوا أن دمها هدر» (أبو داود ٤٣٦١، وصححه الألباني، ونحوه عند النسائي ٤٠٧٥). قتل رجل أم أولاده، وهي أَمَةٌ يملكها، بسبب كلام، وأبطل النبي حتى ديتها. ويستدل الفقهاء بهذا الحديث على قتل من يسب النبي. وفي رواية أخرى (أبو داود ٤٣٦٢، ضعيفة الإسناد) أن امرأة يهودية خُنقت، ويبحث العلماء هل هي القصة نفسها أم غيرها.

Women "deficient in intelligence and religion"; majority of Hell
النساء ناقصات عقل ودين وأكثر أهل النار
صحيح البخاري ٣٠٤ · صحيح مسلم ٧٩
Bukhari 304البخاري ٣٠٤ Muslim 79aمسلم ٧٩

On Eid Muhammad passed the women and said: "Give alms, for I have seen that the majority of the dwellers of Hell-fire were you." They asked why. "You curse frequently and are ungrateful to your husbands. I have not seen anyone more deficient in intelligence and religion than you, A cautious sensible man could be led astray by some of you." When they asked what was deficient, he answered: "Is not the testimony of two women equal to that of one man?... That is the deficiency of her intelligence. Doesn't she neither pray nor fast during her menses? That is the deficiency of her religion" (Bukhari 304; Muslim 79). The reasons offered are a legal rule from Quran 2:282 and a ritual exemption God Himself imposes, turned into proof of defect. Apologists argue "aql" means something like judgment, and that the remark is a gentle tease, but the stated conclusion is explicit and was used for centuries to justify discounting women's testimony and authority.

مرّ النبي في العيد بالنساء فقال: «تصدّقن فإني رأيتكن أكثر أهل النار». قلن: ولمَ يا رسول الله؟ قال: «تكثرن اللعن وتكفرن العشير، ما رأيت من ناقصات عقل ودين أذهب للُبّ الرجل الحازم من إحداكن». فلما سألنه عن النقصان قال: «أليس شهادة المرأة مثل نصف شهادة الرجل؟... فذلك من نقصان عقلها. أليس إذا حاضت لم تصلِّ ولم تصم؟ فذلك من نقصان دينها» (البخاري ٣٠٤، ومسلم ٧٩). فالدليلان حكم تشريعي من الآية ٢:٢٨٢ وإعفاء تعبدي يضعه الله نفسه، وقد جُعلا برهاناً على النقص. يقول المدافعون إن العقل هنا بمعنى الضبط، وإن الكلام مداعبة لطيفة، لكن الخلاصة المعلنة صريحة، وقد استُخدمت قروناً لتبرير إنقاص شهادة المرأة وولايتها.

Killed clinging to the Kaaba curtains despite the amnesty
قتل ابن خطل وهو متعلق بأستار الكعبة
صحيح البخاري ٣٠٤٤ · سنن أبي داود ٢٦٨٥ · سنن النسائي ٤٠٧٢
Bukhari 3044البخاري ٣٠٤٤ Abu Dawud 2685أبو داود ٢٦٨٥ Nasa'i 4072النسائي ٤٠٧٢

Anas reports that when Muhammad entered Mecca at the conquest wearing a helmet, a man told him: "Ibn Khatal is clinging to the curtains of the Kaaba." He said, "Kill him" (Bukhari 3044; Abu Dawud 2685 adds that Abu Barzah al-Aslami killed him). Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas reports that the Prophet gave amnesty to the people of Mecca except four men and two women, whom he ordered killed "even if you find them clinging to the covers of the Kaaba" (Nasa'i 4072, graded Sahih by Al-Albani). Ibn Khatal was killed at the holiest sanctuary in Islam, while holding the Kaaba, with no trial. The sources of his alleged crimes (murdering a servant, satirical verses about the Prophet) come from the biographies, while the hadith simply records the order. Bukhari files the report under the chapter on "the killing of a captive".

يروي أنس أن النبي دخل مكة عام الفتح وعلى رأسه المِغفر، فلما نزعه جاءه رجل فقال: «ابن خطل متعلق بأستار الكعبة». فقال: «اقتلوه» (البخاري ٣٠٤٤؛ وفي أبي داود ٢٦٨٥ أن أبا برزة الأسلمي قتله). ويروي سعد بن أبي وقاص أن النبي أمّن الناس يوم الفتح إلا أربعة رجال وامرأتين وأمر بقتلهم «وإن وجدتموهم متعلقين بأستار الكعبة» (النسائي ٤٠٧٢، وصححه الألباني). فقُتل ابن خطل عند أقدس مكان في الإسلام وهو ممسك بالكعبة دون محاكمة. وما يُذكر من جرائمه (قتل خادم وهجاء النبي) مصدره كتب السيرة، أما الحديث فلا يسجل إلا الأمر. وقد أورده البخاري في باب «قتل الأسير».

Captive Safiyya allotted, then taken after her people were killed
صفية أسيرة خيبر تُعطى لدحية ثم يتخذها النبي
صحيح البخاري ٤٢٠٠ / ٩٤٧ · سنن أبي داود ٢٩٩٦ · سنن ابن ماجه ١٩٥٧
Bukhari 4200البخاري ٤٢٠٠ Bukhari 947البخاري ٩٤٧ Abu Dawud 2996أبو داود ٢٩٩٦ Ibn Majah 1957ابن ماجه ١٩٥٧

Anas reports that after the Prophet declared "Khaybar is ruined", the people ran into the streets, "their fighters were killed, and their children and women were taken captive". Safiyya was among them. She first fell to the share of Dihya al-Kalbi, and then came to the Messenger of Allah, who "made her manumission her mahr (dowry)" (Bukhari 4200, 947; Abu Dawud 2996, graded Sahih by Al-Albani; Ibn Majah 1957). Biographers (Ibn Ishaq and others) record that her father and her husband were killed by the Muslims. Nothing in the hadiths describes a choice she could have made: a woman captured in a raid that killed her men, allotted like property, and married on the same expedition. Apologists argue that she accepted and was honored, and some biographical reports say she was offered a choice; but that choice was made as a captive whose people had just been killed.

يروي أنس أن النبي بعد أن قال «خربت خيبر» خرج أهلها إلى السكك، «فقُتلت المقاتلة وسُبيت الذرية والنساء»، وكانت صفية بينهن. وقعت أولاً في سهم دحية الكلبي ثم صارت إلى رسول الله، «وجعل عتقها صداقها» (البخاري ٤٢٠٠، ٩٤٧؛ أبو داود ٢٩٩٦ وصححه الألباني؛ ابن ماجه ١٩٥٧). ويذكر كتّاب السيرة (ابن إسحاق وغيره) أن أباها وزوجها قُتلا على أيدي المسلمين. ولا يصف أي حديث خياراً كان في وسعها: امرأة سُبيت في غارة قُتل فيها رجالها، وقُسّمت كالمتاع، وتزوجها النبي في الحملة نفسها. يقول المدافعون إنها قبلت وأُكرمت، وتذكر بعض روايات السيرة أنها خُيّرت، لكنه خيار اتخذته أسيرة قُتل قومها قبل أيام.

Umar ibn al-Khattab reports from the Prophet: "A man will not be asked why he beat his wife" (Abu Dawud 2147; Ibn Majah 1986). In Ibn Majah the narrator al-Ash'ath was a guest in Umar's house when Umar struck his wife during the night and al-Ash'ath separated them; Umar then told him this saying. The grading is disputed: Al-Albani rates it weak, while Zubair Ali Zai rates the chain hasan, and it is included in Mishkat al-Masabih (3268). Read alongside Quran 4:34 and Bukhari 5204, critics read the rule as saying a husband is not called to account for striking his wife. Defenders cite Bukhari 5204 and other sayings that condemn beating a wife as one beats a slave.

عن عمر بن الخطاب عن النبي: «لا يُسأل الرجل فيمَ ضرب امرأته» (أبو داود ٢١٤٧، ابن ماجه ١٩٨٦). وفي ابن ماجه أن الأشعث كان ضيفاً في بيت عمر فضرب عمر امرأته ليلاً فحجز بينهما الأشعث، فحدّثه عمر بهذا. والحكم عليه مختلف: ضعّفه الألباني وحسّن إسناده الزبير علي زئي، وأورده صاحب مشكاة المصابيح (٣٢٦٨). ومع الآية ٤:٣٤ والبخاري ٥٢٠٤ يرى النقاد أن القاعدة تعني أن الزوج لا يُسأل عن ضربه زوجته. ويحتج المدافعون بالبخاري ٥٢٠٤ وبأحاديث أخرى تذم ضرب الزوجة كما يُضرب العبد.

Prostration is the act of worship reserved for God, so the saying places a husband just below God in the hierarchy of the household. Apologists stress that it is hypothetical and that Muslims may not prostrate to anyone but God, but the stated reason is the husband's rank over his wife, which Quran 2:228 ("men have a degree over them") and 4:34 ("men are in charge of women") also teach.

يروي أبو هريرة أن النبي قال: «لو كنت آمراً أحداً أن يسجد لأحد لأمرت المرأة أن تسجد لزوجها» (جامع الترمذي ١١٥٩ وحسّنه وصححه الألباني، وكذا ابن ماجه ١٨٥٣). والسجود عبادة مخصوصة لله، فيضع القول الزوج في المرتبة التي تلي الله في هرم الأسرة. يؤكد المدافعون أن الكلام افتراضي وأن السجود لغير الله محرم، لكن العلة المذكورة هي علو منزلة الزوج على زوجته، وهو ما تقرره الآيتان ٢:٢٢٨ («وللرجال عليهن درجة») و٤:٣٤ («الرجال قوامون على النساء»).

The Arabic taqtil is an intensive form meaning thorough, merciless killing, and the verse says it applies "wherever they are found". Classical exegesis (al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir) explains the punishment as exile or killing. It is a Quranic basis for killing people for speech and for suspected disloyalty.

Abu Huraira reports that the Prophet said: "If a husband calls his wife to his bed and she refuses, and he spends the night angry with her, the angels curse her until morning" (Bukhari 3237; Muslim 1436d). A woman's refusal of sex, for any reason, is made a matter of divine cursing, with no exception stated in the text for illness, exhaustion or fear. The rule runs one way: it names the wife's refusal, never the husband's insistence. Apologists say it applies only when the wife has no valid excuse, and that it is about marital harmony, but the report states no excuse and leaves consent to the husband's call.

يروي أبو هريرة أن النبي قال: «إذا دعا الرجل امرأته إلى فراشه فأبت، فبات غضبان عليها، لعنتها الملائكة حتى تصبح» (البخاري ٣٢٣٧، مسلم ١٤٣٦د). فيجعل الحديث رفض المرأة للجماع، لأي سبب، مسألة لعن إلهي، دون أن يذكر النص استثناءً للمرض أو التعب أو الخوف. والقاعدة تسير في اتجاه واحد: فهي تذكر رفض الزوجة ولا تذكر إلحاح الزوج. يقول المدافعون إنها تنطبق فقط حين لا عذر للمرأة وإن المقصود المودة الزوجية، لكن الحديث لا يذكر عذراً ويترك الأمر لدعوة الزوج.

صحيح البخاري ٦٨٤١ · صحيح مسلم ١٦٩٩

Jews brought a man and a woman who had committed adultery to Muhammad. He asked what the Torah says about stoning; they said the penalty was public disgrace and flogging. Abdullah ibn Salam told them they were lying, the stoning verse was found in the Torah, and "the Messenger of Allah ordered that the two be stoned to death" (Bukhari 6841; Muslim 1699a). Ibn Umar adds: "I saw the man leaning over the woman to protect her from the stones." The Prophet enforced death by stoning on two non-Muslims on the strength of their own scripture, and the story is cited as precedent in the Islamic penal code. The couple were executed for consensual sex, and the report records the man's attempt to shield her as he was killed.

جاء اليهود برجل وامرأة زنيا إلى النبي فسألهم عن حكم الرجم في التوراة، فقالوا: التحميم والجلد. فقال عبد الله بن سلام: كذبتم، إن فيها آية الرجم، فوُجدت، «فأمر بهما رسول الله فرُجما» (البخاري ٦٨٤١، مسلم ١٦٩٩أ). ويضيف ابن عمر: «فرأيت الرجل يَحني على المرأة يقيها الحجارة». نفّذ النبي حكم الرجم بحق غير مسلمين اعتماداً على كتابهم، ويُستدل بالقصة سابقةً في نظام العقوبات الإسلامي. فقُتل الاثنان لعلاقة بالتراضي، وسجّل الحديث محاولة الرجل حماية المرأة وهو يُقتل.

Mu'awiyah reports the Prophet's command: "Whoever drinks wine, flog him. If he returns to it, flog him. If he returns to it, flog him. If he returns on the fourth time, kill him" (Abu Dawud 4482, graded Hasan Sahih by Al-Albani; Tirmidhi 1444, graded Hasan by Darussalam). A man can be put to death for a fourth conviction of drinking alcohol, an offense with no victim. Tirmidhi reports that the ruling was later abrogated, that a man brought a fourth time was lashed but not killed, and that most jurists do not apply it. The command remains in two of the six canonical books, graded authentic, and the existence of an abrogation shows the original command was once the law.

يروي معاوية أمر النبي: «من شرب الخمر فاجلدوه، فإن عاد فاجلدوه، فإن عاد فاجلدوه، فإن عاد في الرابعة فاقتلوه» (أبو داود ٤٤٨٢ وحسّنه وصححه الألباني، الترمذي ١٤٤٤ وحسّنه). فيُقتل الإنسان في المرة الرابعة لشرب الكحول، وهو فعل لا ضحية فيه. ويذكر الترمذي أن الحكم نُسخ لاحقاً، وأن رجلاً أُتي به في الرابعة فجُلد ولم يُقتل، وأن أكثر الفقهاء لا يعملون به. لكن الأمر يبقى في كتابين من الكتب الستة صحيح الإسناد، ووجود النسخ دليل على أنه كان حكماً نافذاً.

"O Prophet, strive against the disbelievers and the hypocrites and be harsh upon them. Their refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination." The identical command appears in two suras (9:73 and 66:9), addressed to Muhammad, and covers both outsiders (disbelievers) and professed Muslims who are insincere (hypocrites). Classical commentators (al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir) explain "jihad" here as the sword against disbelievers and the tongue and hand, or legal punishment, against hypocrites. The verse mandates harshness as a divine command, not a reaction to attack. Apologists say jihad means "striving" in general, but the context sets out war and Hell for the target group.

«يَا أَيُّهَا النَّبِيُّ جَاهِدِ الْكُفَّارَ وَالْمُنَافِقِينَ وَاغْلُظْ عَلَيْهِمْ ۚ وَمَأْوَاهُمْ جَهَنَّمُ ۖ وَبِئْسَ الْمَصِيرُ». ويرد الأمر نفسه في سورتين (٩:٧٣ و٦٦:٩) موجهاً إلى محمد، ويشمل الخارجين عن الدين (الكفار) والمنتسبين إلى الإسلام غير الصادقين (المنافقين). ويفسر المفسرون الأوائل (الطبري وابن كثير) الجهاد هنا بالسيف على الكفار وباللسان واليد أو بالعقوبة على المنافقين. فالآية توجب الغلظة أمراً إلهياً لا ردّاً على اعتداء. يقول المدافعون إن الجهاد يعني «بذل الجهد» عموماً، لكن السياق يقرن الأمر بالحرب وبجهنم للفئة المستهدفة.

"They wish you would disbelieve as they disbelieved so you would be alike. So do not take allies from among them until they emigrate for the cause of Allah. But if they turn away, then seize them and kill them wherever you find them, and take neither ally nor helper from among them." The verse is about people who left Islam or refuse to emigrate to Medina (the "hypocrites" of 4:88), and it commands their capture and execution anywhere. The next verse (4:90) exempts those who join a people with whom the Muslims have a treaty, or who come to them with hearts unwilling to fight either side. Some classical jurists cited this verse in support of killing apostates. The default is death for turning away, the exceptions are narrow.

«وَدُّوا لَوْ تَكْفُرُونَ كَمَا كَفَرُوا فَتَكُونُونَ سَوَاءً ۖ فَلَا تَتَّخِذُوا مِنْهُمْ أَوْلِيَاءَ حَتَّىٰ يُهَاجِرُوا فِي سَبِيلِ اللَّهِ ۚ فَإِن تَوَلَّوْا فَخُذُوهُمْ وَاقْتُلُوهُمْ حَيْثُ وَجَدتُّمُوهُمْ ۖ وَلَا تَتَّخِذُوا مِنْهُمْ وَلِيًّا وَلَا نَصِيرًا». تتحدث الآية عن قوم تركوا الإسلام أو أبوا الهجرة إلى المدينة («منافقو» الآية ٤:٨٨)، وتأمر بأخذهم وقتلهم في أي مكان. وتستثني الآية التالية (٤:٩٠) من يصلون إلى قوم بينهم وبين المسلمين ميثاق، أو جاؤوا حصرت صدورهم عن قتال المسلمين أو قتال قومهم. وقد احتج بعض الفقهاء بها على قتل المرتدين. فالأصل القتل لمن تولّى، والاستثناءات ضيقة.

Quran 9:123القرآن ٩:١٢٣

"O you who believe, fight those of the disbelievers who are near you, and let them find harshness in you, and know that Allah is with the righteous." This verse, among the last revealed, orders the Muslims to fight the disbelievers closest to them in turn, creating a rolling frontier of war, and demands harshness (ghilza) as a trait. Classical commentators use it to organize the order of conquest: first the nearest enemy, then the next. The command is not conditioned on aggression by the enemy. Apologists say it applies to the specific situation of the Arab tribes, but the verse itself states a general rule for believers.

«يَا أَيُّهَا الَّذِينَ آمَنُوا قَاتِلُوا الَّذِينَ يَلُونَكُم مِّنَ الْكُفَّارِ وَلْيَجِدُوا فِيكُمْ غِلْظَةً ۚ وَاعْلَمُوا أَنَّ اللَّهَ مَعَ الْمُتَّقِينَ». تأمر هذه الآية، وهي من أواخر ما نزل، المسلمين بقتال الكفار الأقرب إليهم تباعاً، فتنشئ جبهة حرب متنقلة، وتطلب الغلظة صفةً. ويستخدمها المفسرون الأوائل لترتيب الفتوح: الأقرب فالأبعد. والأمر غير مشروط باعتداء العدو. يقول المدافعون إنه خاص بظروف القبائل العربية، لكن الآية تقرر قاعدة عامة للمؤمنين.

الشجر يقول: يا مسلم هذا يهودي ورائي فتعال فاقتله
صحيح مسلم ٢٩٢٢
Muslim 2922مسلم ٢٩٢٢

Muslim 2922 (Abu Hurayra): "The Last Hour would not come until the Muslims fight the Jews and the Muslims kill them, until the Jews hide behind a stone or a tree and the stone or tree says: Muslim, servant of Allah, there is a Jew behind me, come and kill him, except the gharqad tree, for it is the tree of the Jews." The hadith is often quoted in political rhetoric, and the Hamas charter of 1988 cites it. Apologists point out that it is an end-times report, not a command, that it describes a future battle, and that it does not appear in the Quran. The objection is that it is a canonical, unqualified statement presenting the killing of Jews as an expected sign of the Hour, with even inanimate objects taking part.

في مسلم ٢٩٢٢ عن أبي هريرة: «لا تقوم الساعة حتى يقاتل المسلمون اليهود فيقتلهم المسلمون حتى يختبئ اليهودي من وراء الحجر والشجر، فيقول الحجر أو الشجر: يا مسلم يا عبد الله هذا يهودي خلفي فتعال فاقتله، إلا الغرقد فإنه من شجر اليهود». ويُستشهد بالحديث كثيراً في الخطاب السياسي، وقد استُشهد به في ميثاق حماس عام ١٩٨٨. ويرد المدافعون بأنه خبر عن آخر الزمان وليس أمراً، وأنه يصف معركة مستقبلية، وأنه ليس في القرآن. والاعتراض أنه نص معتمد مطلق يجعل قتل اليهود علامة منتظرة من علامات الساعة، حتى إن الجمادات تشارك فيه.

Muslim 2167a (Abu Hurayra): "Do not greet the Jews and the Christians before they greet you, and when you meet any one of them on the roads, force him to go to the narrowest part of it." Many jurists used this to justify a lower public status for non-Muslims. Some apologists argue that it was specific to the circumstances of the Banu Qurayza, who had broken their treaty, and that the Quran (60:8) permits kindness toward peaceful non-Muslims; some modern scholars read it as being about etiquette on narrow roads. The hadith as reported, however, names Jews and Christians in general and gives no such reason.

في مسلم ٢١٦٧أ عن أبي هريرة: «لا تبدؤوا اليهود والنصارى بالسلام، وإذا لقيتم أحدهم في طريق فاضطرّوه إلى أضيقه». وقد استعمله كثير من الفقهاء لتبرير منزلة عامة أدنى لغير المسلمين. ويرى بعض المدافعين أنه خاص بظروف بني قريظة الذين نقضوا العهد، وأن القرآن (٦٠:٨) يجيز البرّ بغير المسلمين المسالمين، ويحمله بعض المعاصرين على آداب الطريق الضيق. غير أن الحديث كما روي يذكر اليهود والنصارى عامة ولا يذكر هذا السبب.

Muslim 1767aمسلم ١٧٦٧أ

Muslim 1767a quotes Umar ibn al-Khattab saying he heard the Prophet say: "I will expel the Jews and Christians from the Arabian Peninsula and will not leave any but Muslim." Umar later carried this out. Islamic law since then has generally treated the Hijaz as closed to the open practice of other religions, a rule still enforced today in Saudi Arabia, where non-Muslim worship in public is banned. Apologists say the order was a political security measure against groups who had sided with the Prophet's enemies, and that Arabia is a special sanctuary. The objection is that the text states it as a general religious rule, not as a response to named treason.

يروي مسلم ١٧٦٧أ عن عمر بن الخطاب أنه سمع النبي يقول: «لأُخرجنّ اليهود والنصارى من جزيرة العرب فلا أترك فيها إلا مسلماً». وقد نفّذ عمر ذلك لاحقاً. وقد اعتبر الفقه الإسلامي بعد ذلك الحجاز عموماً مغلقاً أمام الممارسة العلنية لغير الإسلام، وهي قاعدة ما زالت مطبقة في السعودية حيث تُحظر العبادة العلنية لغير المسلمين. ويقول المدافعون إن الأمر إجراء سياسي أمني ضد جماعات انحازت لأعداء النبي، وإن الجزيرة حرم خاص. والاعتراض أن النص يذكره قاعدة دينية عامة لا ردّاً على خيانة مسماة.

Muslim 510aمسلم ٥١٠أ

In Muslim 510a Abu Dharr reports that if a worshipper has nothing in front of him as tall as the back of a saddle, his prayer is cut off by a donkey, a woman or a black dog, and the Prophet said "the black dog is a devil." Placing a woman in the same list as a donkey and a dog is the moral problem. Most jurists read "cuts off" as meaning it breaks the worshipper's concentration, not that it cancels the prayer, though some (such as the Hanbali school, for the black dog) took it literally. Aisha is reported to have objected to the comparison in other narrations, which is a point for the apologists. The text of this hadith itself still carries the comparison.

في مسلم ٥١٠أ عن أبي ذر أن المصلي إذا لم يكن بين يديه مثل مؤخرة الرحل قطع صلاته الحمار والمرأة والكلب الأسود، وقال النبي: «الكلب الأسود شيطان». والإشكال الأخلاقي في جعل المرأة في قائمة واحدة مع الحمار والكلب. ويحمل أكثر الفقهاء «القطع» على قطع الخشوع لا إبطال الصلاة، وأخذه بعضهم على ظاهره (كالحنابلة في الكلب الأسود). وقد رُوي اعتراض عائشة على هذه المقارنة في روايات أخرى، وهذا مما يحتج به المدافعون. لكن نص هذا الحديث يبقى حاملاً للمقارنة.

Abu Dawud 495 (Abdullah ibn Amr; graded hasan sahih by Al-Albani): "Command your children to pray when they become seven years old and beat them for it when they become ten years old, and arrange their beds separately." Beating a ten-year-old child over a religious act is the moral problem. Classical jurists generally limited the beating to a light, non-injuring strike, and some scholars argue it is only permitted to a parent and only as a last resort. The hadith itself sets no such limit.

في أبي داود ٤٩٥ عن عبد الله بن عمرو (وحسّنه الألباني وصححه): «مروا أولادكم بالصلاة وهم أبناء سبع سنين، واضربوهم عليها وهم أبناء عشر، وفرّقوا بينهم في المضاجع». والإشكال الأخلاقي ضرب طفل في العاشرة على أمر ديني. وقد قيّد الفقهاء عموماً الضرب بأن يكون خفيفاً غير مبرّح، ويرى بعض المعاصرين أنه للوالد وحده وكآخر وسيلة. لكن الحديث نفسه لا يضع هذا القيد.

Muslim 2240b (Abu Hurayra): the one who kills a gecko with the first stroke is credited with one hundred virtues, with the second stroke fewer, and with the third fewer again. The hadith puts a score on how many blows it takes, so it rewards killing the animal quickly and fully, and the reward drops each time it survives a blow. Defenders say geckos were regarded as vermin and the reward is for efficient killing, which is a mercy to the animal, and that other hadith (not checked here) say the gecko blew on the fire thrown at Abraham. The objection is that a hundred good deeds for killing a harmless, insect-eating animal is a very large reward for an act with no real benefit, and in conflict with the Quran's view of animals as "communities like you" (6:38).

في مسلم ٢٢٤٠ب عن أبي هريرة: من قتل وزغة في أول ضربة كُتبت له مائة حسنة، وفي الثانية دون ذلك، وفي الثالثة دون ذلك. فالحديث يحدد درجة الثواب بعدد الضربات، فيكافئ قتل الحيوان بسرعة وتمام، وينقص الأجر كلما نجا من ضربة. ويقول المدافعون إن الوزغ كان يُعد من الحشرات المؤذية وإن الثواب على إحسان القتلة رحمة بالحيوان، وإن أحاديث أخرى (لم أتحقق منها هنا) تقول إنه نفخ في النار التي أُلقي فيها إبراهيم. والاعتراض أن مائة حسنة لقتل حيوان غير مؤذٍ يأكل الحشرات ثواب كبير على فعل لا نفع حقيقياً فيه، وأنه يخالف نظرة القرآن إلى الحيوانات بأنها «أُمَمٌ أَمْثَالُكُم» (٦:٣٨).

Tirmidhi 1486 (Abdullah ibn Mughaffal): "If it were not that dogs were a nation among the nations, I would order that all of them be killed, so kill every one of them that is all black." Tirmidhi calls it hasan sahih and Al-Albani grades it sahih, but Zubair Ali Zai grades the chain in the Abu Dawud, Nasa'i and Ibn Majah versions as weak. Apologists say the order was a temporary measure against stray dogs and rabies, and that the hadith itself recognises dogs as a nation. The objection is that it orders the killing of a whole class of animals by colour, and that the explanation given in other narrations (Muslim 510a, on this page, calls the black dog a devil) is theological, not medical.

في الترمذي ١٤٨٦ عن عبد الله بن مغفل: «لولا أن الكلاب أمة من الأمم لأمرت بقتلها كلها، فاقتلوا منها كل أسود بهيم». وقال الترمذي حسن صحيح، وصححه الألباني، لكن زبير علي زئي ضعّف إسناده في روايات أبي داود والنسائي وابن ماجه. ويقول المدافعون إن الأمر كان مؤقتاً لمواجهة الكلاب الضالة والكَلَب، وإن الحديث نفسه يعدّ الكلاب أمة. والاعتراض أنه يأمر بقتل صنف كامل من الحيوانات بحسب لونه، وأن التعليل في روايات أخرى (مسلم ٥١٠أ في هذه الصفحة يجعل الكلب الأسود شيطاناً) تعليل عقدي لا طبي.

When Ikrimah asks what the animal has done, Ibn Abbas says he thinks the Prophet disliked its flesh being eaten after such a thing. Al-Albani grades the hadith hasan sahih, but Abu Dawud himself comments that it is not a strong tradition. Apologists say the animal's killing is a way to remove the evidence and protect the community from the animal. The objection is that an animal with no moral responsibility is put to death as a penalty, and that Ibn Abbas gives only his own guess for the reason.

في أبي داود ٤٤٦٤ عن ابن عباس: «من أتى بهيمة فاقتلوه واقتلوها معه». وحين سأل عكرمة عن ذنب البهيمة قال ابن عباس إنه يظن أن النبي كره أن يُؤكل لحمها وقد فُعل بها ذلك. وحسّن الألباني الحديث وصححه، لكن أبا داود نفسه قال: «ليس هذا بالقوي». ويقول المدافعون إن قتل البهيمة لإزالة الدليل وحماية المجتمع منها. والاعتراض أن حيواناً لا مسؤولية أخلاقية عليه يُقتل عقوبة، وأن ابن عباس لا يقدم إلا ظنه سبباً.

Defenders say this warns against cruelty to animals and may reflect a temporary punishment for a person with other sins. The objection is that the hadith names the cat as the reason for Hell, and as reported it offers no other sin, while the same religion treats an eternal punishment as the penalty for disbelief. A reader who accepts the hadith must hold that Allah punishes with Hell fire for neglecting a cat.

Bukhari 25 (Ibn Umar) has the Prophet say: "I have been ordered to fight the people until they testify" that there is no god but Allah and that Muhammad is His messenger, establish the prayer and pay the zakat; once they do, their lives and property are protected except for what the law requires. The Quran says "fight them until there is no fitnah and the religion, all of it, is for Allah" (8:39). Ibn Kathir records several readings of fitnah (shirk, or persecution of Muslims) and cites this hadith under the verse. Apologists, including a report from Ibn Umar attributed to Bukhari, say that the fighting was against persecution while Islam was weak and ended once Islam became strong. The objection is that the hadith as written has no such limit: the stated goal is a profession of faith, and prayer and zakat are conditions for being spared.

في البخاري ٢٥ عن ابن عمر قال النبي: «أُمرت أن أقاتل الناس حتى يشهدوا أن لا إله إلا الله وأن محمداً رسول الله، ويقيموا الصلاة، ويؤتوا الزكاة، فإذا فعلوا ذلك عصموا مني دماءهم وأموالهم إلا بحق الإسلام». ويقول القرآن: «وَقَاتِلُوهُمْ حَتَّىٰ لَا تَكُونَ فِتْنَةٌ وَيَكُونَ الدِّينُ كُلُّهُ لِلَّهِ» (٨:٣٩). وينقل ابن كثير أقوالاً في معنى الفتنة (الشرك، أو اضطهاد المسلمين) ويورد هذا الحديث عند الآية. ويقول المدافعون، ومنهم أثر عن ابن عمر ينسبه ابن كثير إلى البخاري، إن القتال كان ضد الاضطهاد حين كان الإسلام ضعيفاً وانتهى لما قوي. والاعتراض أن الحديث بنصه لا يذكر هذا القيد: فالغاية النطق بالشهادة، وإقامة الصلاة وإيتاء الزكاة شرطان للنجاة.

"And prepare against them whatever you are able of power and of steeds of war by which you may terrify (turhibuna) the enemy of Allah and your enemy and others besides them whom you do not know." Ibn Kathir says Muslims must prepare for war against the disbelievers as far as they are able, defines "power" through the hadith "power is shooting," and records that scholars disagree about who the unnamed "others" are (the Banu Qurayza, the Persians, or the hypocrites). Apologists say this is about deterrence, so that war is avoided, and the next verse (8:61) says to incline to peace if the enemy does. The objection is that the verse makes terrifying others the stated purpose of military preparation, and leaves the group of "others" open.

«وَأَعِدُّوا لَهُم مَّا اسْتَطَعْتُم مِّن قُوَّةٍ وَمِن رِّبَاطِ الْخَيْلِ تُرْهِبُونَ بِهِ عَدُوَّ اللَّهِ وَعَدُوَّكُمْ وَآخَرِينَ مِن دُونِهِمْ لَا تَعْلَمُونَهُمُ اللَّهُ يَعْلَمُهُمْ». ويقول ابن كثير إن على المسلمين الاستعداد لحرب الكفار بقدر طاقتهم، ويفسّر «القوة» بحديث «ألا إن القوة الرمي»، وينقل اختلاف العلماء في «الآخرين» (بنو قريظة أو الفرس أو المنافقون). ويقول المدافعون إن المقصود الردع لتجنب الحرب، وإن الآية التالية (٨:٦١) تأمر بالجنوح للسلم إن جنح العدو. والاعتراض أن الآية تجعل إرهاب الآخرين الغاية المعلنة للاستعداد العسكري، وتترك «الآخرين» دون تحديد.

لا تحل له حتى تنكح زوجاً غيره
٢:٢٣٠ (البقرة)
Quran 2:230القرآن ٢:٢٣٠ Ibn Kathir on 2:230ابن كثير ٢:٢٣٠

If a husband divorces his wife for the third time, "she is not lawful to him afterwards until she marries a husband other than him" (2:230); only if that husband divorces her may the first couple remarry. Ibn Kathir explains that the second marriage must be consummated, citing a hadith in which the Prophet says the woman is not lawful to her first husband "until he enjoys her 'usaylah (sexual relation)," and he adds that a marriage arranged only to make her lawful again (tahlil) is cursed. Defenders say the rule is a deterrent against hasty triple divorce and that the tahlil trick is condemned. The objection is that the penalty falls on the woman, who must be married to and have intercourse with another man, while the man who pronounced the divorce loses only the marriage.

«فَإِن طَلَّقَهَا فَلَا تَحِلُّ لَهُ مِن بَعْدُ حَتَّىٰ تَنكِحَ زَوْجًا غَيْرَهُ فَإِن طَلَّقَهَا فَلَا جُنَاحَ عَلَيْهِمَا أَن يَتَرَاجَعَا» (٢:٢٣٠). ويبين ابن كثير أن الزواج الثاني لا بد أن يكون بدخول، ويذكر حديثاً قال فيه النبي إنها لا تحل للأول «حتى يذوق عُسيلتها» (الجماع)، ويضيف أن الزواج المدبّر لمجرد التحليل ملعون. ويقول المدافعون إن الحكم رادع عن الطلاق الثلاث المتسرع وإن حيلة التحليل مدانة. والاعتراض أن العقوبة تقع على المرأة التي يجب أن تتزوج رجلاً آخر وتجامعه، بينما لا يخسر من أوقع الطلاق إلا الزواج.

In Muslim 1852a 'Arfaja reports the Prophet saying that "different evils will make their appearance in the near future," and "anyone who tries to disrupt the affairs of this Umma while they are united, you should strike him with the sword, whoever he be." The translation on the page adds in parentheses that the offender is to be killed if he does not desist after remonstrance. The hadith is cited as one of the proof-texts for killing those who split the community. Apologists say it concerns armed rebellion that threatens the unity of the state, not peaceful disagreement. The objection is that the text names "anyone" who disrupts unity and does not say the person must be armed or violent.

Section I

Vedic Hinduism ↔ Zoroastrianism

Proto-Indo-Iranian Shared Heritage · 2000 BCE
Historical Foundation
Vedic Hinduism and Avestan Zoroastrianism are two branches of a single original religion practiced c. 2000 BCE on the Eurasian Steppes. When the Indo-Iranians split — one branch entering the Indian subcontinent, one settling the Iranian plateau — they carried virtually identical gods, rituals, sacred drinks, and fire cults. Zarathustra's reform (c. 1200–1000 BCE) performed the most dramatic theological inversion in ancient history: Vedic Devas (divine gods) became Avestan Daevas (demons); Vedic Asuras became Avestan Ahuras (holy beings). Vedic Sanskrit and Avestan are so structurally close that the Rigveda and Avesta can be translated into each other with near-phonetic regularity — this is not metaphor but documented historical linguistics (Comparative Indo-European Philology, as established by Franz Bopp, Max Müller, and confirmed by modern scholars including Martin West and Calvert Watkins).
Vedic Hinduism · Rigveda
Soma
Sacred plant pressed into the divine drink of immortality — hymned in 120 Rigvedic hymns including the entirety of Mandala IX (114 hymns exclusively devoted to Soma). Deified as Soma-deva, the moon-god and immortalizing nectar. Central to all Vedic yajnas; Agni and Indra drink it. Scholars identify it with Ephedra sinica or Peganum harmala — a psychoactive plant whose effects evoke the visionary divine sight celebrated in the Rigveda.
PIE *sauma- · Identical Cognate
⟷
Zoroastrianism · Avesta
Haoma
Linguistically identical (PIE *sauma-). Pressed in the Yasna liturgy; Haoma is simultaneously the plant, the ritual drink, and the divine Yazata Hom. The Hom Yasht (Yasna 9–11) hymns Haoma in the same mode as Rigvedic Soma hymns. Even the preparation ritual — plant pounded on a mortar stone, strained through wool, mixed with milk — is described identically in both traditions. The Vendidad later condemned the drunken use of the plant but retained the ritual. This identity is not coincidence; it is shared religious ancestry preserved in parallel for 3,000 years.
Vedic Hinduism · Rigveda
Agni — Sacred Fire
The second most-hymned deity of the Rigveda (over 200 hymns; Mandala I, II, X). Divine intermediary between humans and gods — the fire altar carries offerings to the heavens. Agnihotra (daily fire offering) and the Agnicayana (fire-altar construction to precise astronomical specifications) are humanity's oldest documented mathematical-ritual technologies. Atharvan priests are the hereditary fire specialists — the word Atharvan itself means "fire priest."
PIE *h1egnis · Cognate Root
⟷
Zoroastrianism · Avesta
Atar — Sacred Fire
Son of Ahura Mazda; the most sacred symbol of divine truth (Asha). Zoroastrian Athravan priests (cognate with Vedic Atharvan) maintain eternal flames in fire temples (ateshgahs). Three grades of sacred fire exist: Atash Bahram (highest, requires 16 different fire sources), Atash Adaran, and Atash Dadgah — directly mirroring the Vedic three-fire system (Garhapatya, Ahavaniya, Dakshinagni). Even the prohibition against contaminating the fire with polluting substances is structurally identical in both traditions.
Vedic Hinduism · Rigveda
Rta — Cosmic Order
The fundamental principle of cosmic truth, moral order, and natural law. Varuna and Mitra are its divine guardians; to violate Rta is the original Vedic conception of moral wrong. Rta governs the movements of celestial bodies, the proper conduct of sacrifice, and human ethics simultaneously — it is simultaneously physics and morality. Evolves into Dharma in later Hinduism. The Rigveda (1.105) calls Rta "the foundation of the universe."
PIE *Hr̥tas "fitted together, true"
⟷
Zoroastrianism · Gathas
Asha — Truth / Cosmic Order
The supreme principle of Ahura Mazda — truth, righteousness, and cosmic order. Phonological and semantic cognate of Vedic Rta (both from PIE *Hr̥tas). Asha Vahishta (Best Truth) is the second Amesha Spenta. Its opposite, Druj (the Lie), is the force of cosmic disorder. This Zoroastrian binary of Asha vs Druj — cosmic truth vs cosmic falsehood — is the direct conceptual ancestor of the Abrahamic Good vs Evil framework, which all three Abrahamic faiths inherited wholesale. The most consequential philosophical export in human religious history traces back to this Vedic Rta concept.
Vedic Hinduism · Rigveda
Varuna & Mitra
The most ancient Vedic divine dyad. Varuna: omniscient lord of cosmic waters, guardian of Rta, divine judge who watches human conduct through his thousand eyes. He releases those who confess error — a precursor to the confession/forgiveness concept. Mitra: covenant, friendship, and light. Their paired names appear in the Mitanni treaty inscription (Kikkuli text, c. 1380 BCE) — the oldest documented mention of Vedic deities, proving their antiquity by archaeological evidence independent of scripture.
Mitanni Treaty 1380 BCE — Hard Archaeological Proof
⟷
Zoroastrianism · Avesta
Ahura Mazda & Mithra
Ahura Mazda ("Wise Lord") = Asura + Mazda — cognate with Vedic Varuna (both titled "Asura/Ahura" = "mighty lord"). Mithra (cognate with Vedic Mitra) became a major Yazata and later spread west as the Roman mystery cult Mithras, worshipped from Britain to Bactria concurrent with early Christianity. Zarathustra's elevation of Ahura Mazda to sole supreme deity — drawn from the Vedic henotheistic framework — is the monotheistic step that influenced all subsequent Abrahamic conceptions of a single God above all other powers.
Vedic Hinduism · Rigveda
Yama — Lord of Death
First mortal to die — becomes lord of the ancestral realm and judge of the dead. Twin of Yami. His two dogs (Shyama and Shabala) guard the path to his realm. The Katha Upanishad's dialogue between the boy Nachiketa and Yama is one of humanity's oldest philosophical discussions of death — predating Plato's Phaedo by at least two centuries. Yama's realm is morally organized: the virtuous go to his bright realm (Pitrloka), the evil to darkness.
PIE *Yemo- "twin" · Identical Etymology
⟷
Zoroastrianism · Avesta
Yima / Jamshid
Etymologically identical to Vedic Yama (PIE *Yemo-). In the Avesta's Vidaidad (Vendidad), Yima is the first mortal who creates a subterranean paradise (vara) sheltering the righteous from a coming cosmic winter — a preserved garden of the pure. He becomes the legendary king Jamshid of Persian tradition. Both Yama and Yima are the same Proto-Indo-Iranian deity of death and judgment, bifurcated by the Hindu-Zoroastrian schism and preserved for 3,000 years in mirror-image form, proving a common source that predates both traditions.
Vedic Hinduism
Devas & Asuras
In the Rigveda, Devas are the luminous gods (Indra, Agni, Varuna, Mitra, Surya) and Asuras hold divine power ambiguously — both words initially denoting the highest divine authority. Over time the Vedic tradition increasingly demonized Asuras. The Deva-Asura war (Devāsura Samgrama) became the central cosmic myth of the Puranas. Vedic Indra, Rudra (Shiva), and the Nasatyas are among the most revered gods — these are specifically the deities Zoroastrianism named as demons.
The Great Inversion — Documented since Max Müller (1823–1900)
⟷
Zoroastrianism · Vendidad
Ahuras & Daevas
Zarathustra's theological revolution: Vedic Devas (divine gods) → Avestan Daevas (demons). Vedic Asuras → Avestan Ahuras (holy beings). The Vendidad law code names Indra, Sarva (=Rudra/Shiva), and Naonhaitya (=Nasatya) as demons — three of the most revered Vedic deities, explicitly condemned by name. This documented inversion is history's strongest evidence that both religions share a common source and then systematically inverted each other's divine hierarchy. The resulting Zoroastrian cosmic dualism — Good vs Evil as supreme cosmic categories — became the most influential philosophical export in Western religious history.
Vedic Hinduism · Rigveda
Mantra & Yajna
Mantra (PIE *mn̥tro- "mental instrument") — sacred verbal formulae with intrinsic cosmic power. Hotar priests recite precise Rigvedic verses to invoke divine presence. Yajna (fire sacrifice; PIE *yaǵ-) is the central act of Vedic religion — a precisely structured ritual with fire, Soma, priestly recitation, and offerings. The wrong syllable in the wrong meter could negate the ritual — liturgical precision is technical necessity, not devotional preference. 1,028 hymns across 10,552 verses preserve this liturgical science.
Hotar = Zaotar · Atharvan = Athravan · PIE Cognates
⟷
Zoroastrianism · Avesta
Manthra & Yasna
Manthra (linguistically identical to Sanskrit Mantra; PIE *mn̥tro-) — sacred words with cosmic power to repel evil. Zaotar priests (cognate with Vedic Hotar) chant the 72-chapter Yasna (cognate with Sanskrit Yajna; PIE *yaǵ-) with equal liturgical precision. The priestly titles are cognate: Vedic Hotar (invoker) = Avestan Zaotar; Vedic Atharvan (fire priest) = Avestan Athravan. Even the liturgical command postures and the requirement for the priest to cover his mouth (to avoid contaminating the sacred fire with breath) have direct Vedic parallels. Scholars Insler, Narten, and Kellens can translate between the two liturgical systems verse by verse.
Vedic Hinduism · Upanishads
Three-Tier Cosmos & Seven Heavens
The Vedic universe: Svarga (heavens), Antariksha (atmosphere), Prithivi (earth). Heavens have seven layers (Saptalokas): Bhuloka, Bhuvarloka, Svarloka, Maharloka, Janarloka, Taparloka, Satyaloka — with Satyaloka (Brahmaloka) being beyond rebirth. The Aitareya Aranyaka describes the soul's post-death ascent through these planes. This precisely layered cosmology establishes the template for all subsequent traditions in the chain.
Seven-plane cosmology — Template for all later traditions
⟷
Zoroastrianism · Bundahishn
Layered Heaven — House of Song
Zoroastrian eschatology: soul ascends through stellar, lunar, and solar planes after death before reaching Garo Demana (House of Song — highest paradise). Later Zoroastrian literature (Bundahishn) elaborated six to seven celestial planes corresponding to grades of righteousness — directly parallel to the Vedic Saptalokas. This layered afterlife entered Judaism via post-exilic literature: the Book of Enoch describes seven heavens in explicit detail; Paul references a "third heaven" (2 Corinthians 12); Islam preserves the seven-heaven structure in Quranic cosmology. The Vedic seven-plane template is the original architectural source.
Vedic Hinduism · Rigveda
Pitrs & Ancestral Spirits
The Pitrs (ancestral spirits) are revered and propitiated through Shraddha rituals. Each person has a divine component that survives death. The concept of a personal divine counterpart — the spirit accompanying the individual — is foundational to Vedic after-death cosmology. The Atharva Veda elaborates a guardian-spirit framework for each living person connected to their ancestral lineage.
Guardian spirit concept — foundational to all subsequent traditions
⟷
Zoroastrianism · Avesta
Fravashi — Guardian Soul
The pre-existent divine guardian spirit of every person — a heavenly prototype that existed before birth, accompanies the living, and survives death. Fravashis of the righteous dead are celebrated at Nowruz (Fravardigan, the feast of the Fravashis). This concept was transmitted directly into post-exilic Judaism and then Christianity as the guardian angel — one of the most universally recognized religious concepts in the Abrahamic world. Mary Boyce (Oxford, 1975): "The guardian angel of later Jewish and Christian tradition is the Zoroastrian Fravashi." The transmission chain is: Vedic Pitrs → Zoroastrian Fravashi → Jewish/Christian guardian angel.
Vedic Hinduism · Rigveda 1.164
Six Periods of Creation
The Vedic cosmogony describes creation proceeding through distinct periods — the Shatapatha Brahmana elaborates six cosmological periods corresponding to six acts of creation. The Rig Vedic Nasadiya Sukta (Hymn of Creation, 10.129) philosophically frames a primordial time before the cosmic order was established. The framework of creation in discrete ordered periods is a distinctly Vedic-Iranian cosmological contribution.
Cosmogonical framework — six-period creation template
⟷
Zoroastrianism · Bundahishn
Six Periods of Creation
Zoroastrian cosmogony describes Ahura Mazda creating the world in six distinct gahanbars (sacred seasonal periods): sky, water, earth, plants, cattle, and humans — each corresponding to a cosmic division of time. The Jewish Encyclopedia (1906) identifies this as a direct parallel to Genesis 1's six days of creation. The structural identity — six ordered creative acts resulting in the inhabited world — reflects the shared Proto-Indo-Iranian cosmogonical framework absorbed by both Zoroastrianism and (via Persian contact) Second Temple Jewish creation theology.

Feature I

Karma — The Original Moral Causality

Rigveda c. 1500 BCE · Predates "Sin" by a millennium
⚖️
Karma vs. Sin — Two Theories of Moral Consequence
The world's oldest moral causality framework versus its Abrahamic theological derivative
Karma (कर्म) — Rigveda to Upanishads
Sanskrit kr ("to act") — first attested in the Rigveda (c. 1500 BCE) as ritual action, its ethical dimension developed in the Upanishads. The Brihadaranyaka Upanishad's Yajnavalkya: "A man becomes good by good action and bad by bad action." Karma is an autonomous impersonal law — like gravity. No external agent rewards or punishes. Actions carry precise consequences across lifetimes. The concept predates any Abrahamic equivalent by a minimum of 700 years and requires no priest, prophet, or divine intermediary.
Sin — Abrahamic Theological Derivative
Sin (Old English synn, from Proto-Germanic *sundjo) is structurally different: not a causal law but a relational violation. It presupposes a divine lawgiver whose commands have been transgressed. Consequences require divine judgment, divine forgiveness, and mediation — sacrifice, prayer, sacrament, repentance. The moral accounting of karma needs no priest. Sin requires the entire ecclesiastical apparatus. Scholars Wendy Doniger and Arvind Sharma note karma offers a more philosophically self-sufficient account of justice: it needs no external agent to function.
Origin: Rigveda c. 1500 BCE — oldest moral causality framework in recorded literature
Origin: Post-exilic Judaism, shaped by Zoroastrian Asha/Druj moral dualism
